utterances.text: But of course, any weapon can be used when the worst comes to the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend about the work of the bakery, you said that its work improved slightly after the reconstruction. Did you mean the reconstruction of the transmission grid, that is, power supply to Foca, because you told us that in late 1993, it improved somewhat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, yes, or perhaps in 1994, the situation was back to normal, and that is what I thought, the electric energy, and also meant the fuel which began to arrive in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, witness. Your Honours, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence here. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for listening to my story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your next witness is Mr. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration which is in the document that the usher is showing you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic, good afternoon. Before I move on to direct examination, I should like to ask you to make a break after you hear my question. We speak the same language and we need that break to leave the interpreters time to interpret the question first. On the screen you have a cursor which writes out words, and when it stops, it means that the interpretation is over and you can begin your answer. So will you please tell me your name?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I am Milomir Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I was born on the 14th of June, 1961, in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And where did you complete your primary and secondary education?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I completed both my primary and secondary education in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And where did you get a job and when?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: In 1984 in the hospital in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you married, do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What part of Foca do you live in?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I live in the part of Foca which is called Cohodar Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the Veselin Maslesa primary school in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. All the way to the eighth grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And was your maths teacher in that school Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your impressions of him as a human being and as a teacher, as you remember him from that period?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I remember him as a good teacher and a good maths teacher, a fair man, fair in marking pupils, and I remember that he tried to help even those pupils who were not good at maths. He tried to make maths more familiar to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us about the ethnic composition of the school, both as regards the staff and the pupils?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, maybe it was 50/50, because that was the ethnic composition of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice that Milorad Krnojelac drew distinctions, differentiated between Muslim and Serb children?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that one of Krnojelac's sons, before the conflict broke out, was the proprietor of the Gong Cafe?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I used to go there occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the period just before the war, let us say late March, early April, did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you see whether Muslim inhabitants of Foca frequented the cafe also at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you remember some of them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Whom you saw there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague from work would drop in with me for a drink or a pizza, Nusret Dzendusic. I used to see Saim, I can't remember his last name, but I know he was a good friend of Spomenka, the owner of the Gong pizza shop, and I also saw others. Irfan Curevac, whom I knew. And of course there were both Serbs and Muslims among the guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of restaurant this was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: It was a coffee shop and a pizza shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In this pizza shop, did you ever hear folk music being played?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No. There were evergreens and rock music.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And was the music loud or soft?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: It was very soft, because I know when I talked to the waiters, they said that the boss did not let them play music loudly while people were eating, eating pizza.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear in this cafe or pizza shop called Gong, that Serbian nationalist songs were sung?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear this being talked about in town?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you -- when were you assigned to the JNA unit in Ustikolina by the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, five or seven days before the conflict in Foca broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this unit in fact the only security for the military depot?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: In the barracks in Ustikolina where I was assigned as a reservist, there were very few soldiers guarding those facilities, and only about 10 or 15 of us reservists responded to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the people who responded to the call-up to go to the JNA in Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: There were both Serbs and Muslims. I knew some of the people. I didn't know others. I used to be in the reserves with Buljubasic, a young man who is a Muslim, and I knew him because we had been in the reserves together before in the 1980s. But in fact the response was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in Ustikolina in this JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 6th of April, and then the commander of this unit which was guarding the depots sent us home because the response had been so poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the commander of this unit, was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992, did you go to work, to your job in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I live in a family house and my father also works in the hospital, and he starts work at 6.00. I start work at 7.00. My father left earlier but he came home and he said, "Don't go. Stay at home." I couldn't go to the hospital because there was some checkpoints on the road. I asked him who told him that, and he replied, "Rasim Kadic, Rasim," who worked in the office with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, when did you go to the hospital for the first time after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Seven or eight days after the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you called to work by the hospital manager?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The hospital manager called me to go to work. His name was Sekula Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you employed in the bookkeeping of the pharmacy in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why they called me, because the head of the pharmacy couldn't get to work. He lived in Miljevina, some 12 kilometres away from Foca. They didn't have the keys, and my office was inside in the pharmacy. That's why they called me, because they had run out of medicines and they needed to intervene or to send medicines to the different wards of the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did your manager then tell you that this was your work obligation, that this was your wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, who appointed the managers and directors of companies after the war broke out? Which organ was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I understand these things, the executive committee of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you were in the hospital, did you meet Milorad Krnojelac there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, we met in the hospital compound. We hadn't seen each other before that. I heard that his house had been burnt down, and I asked him what happened. I tried to comfort him. I said, "Well, you'll build a new house. Don't worry."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you then what his job was at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: He told me that he had been appointed by the executive committee as the manager in the Drina company, and that he had to salvage what could be salvaged of the property that had been destroyed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he ask you to come to the KP Dom to see what could be done about the medicines he found scattered around there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. And I replied that I knew the names of a lot of these medicines, but that it really wasn't my province because I was not a pharmacist and that he should ask Vito Mrgud who was the head of the hospital pharmacy, and he had already arrived to the hospital in Srbinje from Miljevina in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the hospital to go to a military unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Sometime around the 20th or the 22nd. I was at the hospital, and in early May I was called up by the military authorities and sent back to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After you joined the unit, did you visit Foca from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I did visit Foca from time to time when the military authorities let us go, so then I would take a shower, change clothes, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you visited from time to time, did you know that -- was there food, was there bread, were there supplies in the shops in Foca in sufficient quantities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No. The shops were open very rarely, and even when they were, it wasn't food. They were selling other things. And as there was no electricity at that time, all the refrigerators had stopped working so that food supplies were really very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether after the war broke out, most Muslims left Foca together with the Muslim army which withdrew in the direction of Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, yes, I talked to some colleagues over the phone, some Muslim colleagues at the beginning of the war. I talked to some of them, and my wife talked to Mrs. Sikira Cengic, and from these conversations I learnt that a lot of ethnic Muslims had left Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did Sikira tell that to your wife?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you visited Foca, during those visits did you see whether there were non-Serb residents still living there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, yes. In May, in June I would run into some women, some men who used to work with me in my company, for example, Nedziba Sirbubalo, and I talked to him and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether after the war broke out in Foca a curfew was announced?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did it apply to all inhabitants of Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I assumed that it did, except for those who were employed in certain institutions who had to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they have to have special passes to move around during the curfew?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. My father would go to work from 7.00 p.m. till 7.00 in the morning because he worked in shifts, and he had a special pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And during your visits to Foca, did you ever hear in the media or at a rally of some kind that there was a policy of expelling the Muslims, that somebody said that in public?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I never heard that, and in Foca we didn't really have any media. We had Radio Foca, but because there was no electricity, we couldn't really listen to it, so there were very few broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. On your visits to Foca, did you meet Milorad Krnojelac sometimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say exactly how many times, but we would run into each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And who was he with most often, if he was with someone when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I would see him with his colleagues, other teachers, and Zarko Vukovic. He was most often with him. He was a colleague of his, a teacher, a maths teacher from my school. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, cross-examination? Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic, I have a few questions regarding your status as a reserve -- a member of the reserve forces. You said that you were called up before the conflict in Foca broke out. Do you know why there was a call-up before any armed conflict began?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Everybody had an assignment in the peace-time composition, and every year these reserve forces were checked and people were called up to report to their units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And so just so I'm clear on this, there are professional members of the military who are -- whose job it is basically to participate in the military during peace-time as well as wartime, right? That's one category of people?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, these people are not professionals, they were not paid. Simply under the law, they had to do their military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Listen to my question carefully. In the military, there are people who are paid to be soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And then there are also civilians who are in wartime drafted to participate in the military, right? Only in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No. From 1980, when I completed my military service, I was called up ten times to report to this reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Is everybody -- are all -- or were all the men in the former Yugoslavia members of a reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Ninety per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And that meant that if you did your compulsory military service, that you were automatically a member of the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What rank did you have in the reserves?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: A sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And had you wanted -- if you wanted to become a captain, what would you have to do further?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: I had no intention -- I had my job. I would have to spend 10 or 15 days a year in the military only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Again, please listen to my question. If you wanted to be -- if somebody who was a sergeant wanted to become captain, what would he have to do to achieve that rank?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there were schools for reserve officers, so if you were in the regular army doing your service, some people were trained to be ordinary soldiers and this was decided by the military department. It sent people to the army and it sent some people to be regular soldiers, and others to school according to the number of men they needed. Usually -- usually people with university education were sent to become reserve officers, to go to school for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So to become a captain, a person would have to go to more military training than you did, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No. That was when we were doing our military service. If you did your military service for a year and it depends on the time, whether it was in the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s, as part of that, as part of that compulsory military service, if you during that time went to school, you would then be given a rank in the reserves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Would a person automatically become a captain, if he were chosen to go to officer school?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No, no. He would become a second lieutenant, and then from time to time, when the reserves went to do exercises, after every exercise, they would be promoted to a higher rank, one degree up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were those promotions automatic? As long as you went to the exercise, you would achieve the next rank or did you have to do something extra to become promoted?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: No, you didn't have to do anything extra. Everybody was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, the call-up that you described, days before the conflict in Foca started, was it a general call-up for everybody in the reserves? Or was it for specific unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Only for the unit which was guarding the warehouses in Ustikolina. There were perhaps 50 or 60 men in that unit. About other units, I don't know. I have no information as to whether they were mobilised or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said that the response to the call-up was poor. Was the call-up voluntary or was it compulsory?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: It was compulsory, and had there not been a war, the people would probably have suffered consequences under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: If you were -- you were assigned to the unit at Ustikolina, so that means that that's the unit you normally went to as a reserve officer, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MIHAJLOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it was my unit. Everybody was assigned a place to report, and that's where I went to report. Since 1980, I was there seven or eight times, and then twice I went to Hadzici in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume again at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
